card.h1: The Invisible Shield: How Earth Fixed a Hole in the Sky
Mystery at the Bottom of the World
card.p: In Antarctica, three scientists kept seeing numbers so strange that they blamed their machine.

ul.li: Every spring, the ozone reading dropped sharply. They checked the instrument. They checked the data. The low numbers kept returning.
In May 1985, Joe Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jon Shanklin reported that the ozone layer above Antarctica was disappearing each spring.
Class prediction: If a protective layer high above Earth became thinner, what might reach the ground?

card.h1: Earth Wears Sunscreen 15–40 Kilometres Above Us

ul.li: Most atmospheric ozone sits in the stratosphere, roughly 15–40 km above Earth’s surface.
An ozone molecule is three oxygen atoms joined together: O₃. Ordinary oxygen that we breathe is O₂.
The layer is not a solid roof. It is a wide region containing extra ozone molecules, mixed through the air.
Its job: absorb most UVB and all UVC radiation before those invisible rays reach us.

card.h1: UV Is Invisible, but Its Damage Is Not

ul.li: Ultraviolet radiation carries more energy than visible light. You cannot see it, but too much can damage living cells.
For people, extra UVB raises the risk of sunburn, skin cancer and cataracts. It can also damage crops and small organisms in the ocean.
Mini-demo: shine a UV torch on UV-sensitive beads. Cover half with UV-blocking material. The color change makes the invisible visible.
Important distinction: sunscreen protects one person; the ozone layer helps protect life across the planet.

card.h1: A “Safe” Fridge Gas Had a Hidden Journey

ol.li: CFCs were once used in refrigerators, air conditioners, foam and aerosol sprays.
Near the ground, they seemed useful: stable, nonflammable and not very toxic.
That stability let them drift upward for years without breaking apart.
High in the stratosphere, powerful UV light finally split CFC molecules and released chlorine atoms.

card.p: The problem was not where CFCs were used. It was where they eventually traveled.

card.h1: One Chlorine Atom Can Wreck Ozone Again and Again

ol.li: Snatch: chlorine steals one oxygen atom from ozone (O₃), leaving ordinary oxygen (O₂).
Reset: the chlorine later lets go of that oxygen.
Repeat: the same chlorine atom is free to attack another ozone molecule.

card.p: Because chlorine is recycled, one atom can destroy up to 100,000 ozone molecules before another reaction removes it.
Memory hook: not a hammer that breaks once, but a tiny robot that keeps swinging.

card.h1: Why Antarctica Gets a “Hole” Every Spring

ul.li: During the dark Antarctic winter, the stratosphere becomes extremely cold. Special polar clouds form, and reactions on their surfaces prepare chlorine to attack ozone.
When sunlight returns in spring, the reactions speed up and ozone is destroyed rapidly.
The “hole” is not an empty tunnel. It is a huge region where ozone falls below 220 Dobson units.
Winds and temperatures change from year to year, so the hole’s size wiggles even during long-term recovery.

card.h1: The World Made a Planet-Sized Team Decision

ul.li: In 1987, countries agreed to the Montreal Protocol: stop making and using chemicals that destroy ozone.
Every country on Earth eventually ratified the treaty.
Companies redesigned refrigerators, air conditioners, spray products and foams. Governments tightened the rules as scientists learned more.
The result: nearly 99% of banned ozone-depleting substances have been phased out.

card.p: This was not one superhero. It was scientists, citizens, engineers, businesses and governments acting together.

ul.li: The 2025 Antarctic ozone hole was the fifth smallest since 1992. Its average area during peak season was 18.71 million km²: still enormous, but part of a long-term trend toward smaller holes.
Why does healing take decades? Old CFCs survive in the atmosphere for a long time, and chlorine already released does not vanish overnight.
If current rules stay in place, ozone is expected to return to 1980 levels around 2040 for most of the world, 2045 over the Arctic and 2066 over Antarctica.

card.h1: Scientists Still Have to Watch the Sky

ul.li: In 2018, measurements revealed that CFC-11 was declining only half as fast after 2012, pointing to unexpected new emissions.
More observations traced much of the rise to eastern China. By 2019, regional emissions had fallen back to pre-2013 levels.
The lesson: a treaty is not “finished” when it is signed. The atmosphere must be measured, clues investigated and rules enforced.
Ozone detective challenge: What tools could spot an invisible gas? Satellites, weather balloons, ground stations and air samples.

card.h1: Three Smart Moves Beat a Hundred Tiny Gestures

ul.li: Keep cooling gases contained: air conditioners and refrigerators should be serviced by trained technicians. Old equipment must be disposed of properly so refrigerants are recovered, not released.
Look for responsible choices: when adults buy cooling equipment or insulation, ask about ozone-safe, climate-friendly options.
Use sun protection now: healing takes time. Check the UV Index, seek shade, wear protective clothing and use sunscreen.
Share the success story: explain that science found the problem, cooperation changed products, and patient monitoring is repairing the shield.

card.h1: Final Challenge: Build the Ozone Rescue Chain
card.p: In teams, arrange six cards into the true cause-and-effect chain:

ol.li: More harmful UV can reach Earth.
Countries phase out CFCs, and the layer slowly heals.

card.p: Then remove one card and explain what breaks. Finish the sentence: “The ozone story proves that…”

card.h1: A Hole in the Sky Became Proof We Can Repair Harm

ul.li: Remember the shield: ozone high in the stratosphere blocks dangerous UV.
Remember the chain reaction: chlorine from CFCs can destroy ozone again and again.
Remember the comeback: the world changed the rules, nearly eliminated the worst chemicals and put recovery on track.

card.p: Exit ticket: Draw the ozone story in four panels — shield → damage → teamwork → healing.

brief.instruction: Write for curious ten-year-olds in a lively classroom voice: concrete, accurate, and never babyish. Target about 45–55 spoken-support words per slide, with short sentences and memorable comparisons; let the detailed outline supply the substance rather than padding it with generic copy. Define scientific terms on first use. Keep chemical notation simple and pronounceable. Vary sentence and paragraph length. Never use the “Bold term: explanation” list format as the finished slide copy, no signposting such as “Let’s explore,” no sweeping opener, no inspirational summary language, no “not just X, it’s Y” construction, and no em dashes.

Treat this as a colorful picture-book science mystery that becomes a real-world success story. Use smooth flat illustrations, cutaway atmosphere diagrams, oversized molecule characters, a simple chlorine reaction loop, a seasonal Antarctica sequence, a world-cooperation montage, and one clean recovery timeline. Make the invisible visible with rays, shields, layers, arrows and scale comparisons. Preserve scientific distinctions: ozone is a region of gas rather than a solid shell; the hole is severe thinning rather than a literal opening. Use the template’s playful classroom compositions, with act breaks for “So what punched the hole?” and “Your mission.” Keep sourced numbers legible and secondary to the takeaway. Do not turn every slide into a text-filled panel; let the mystery, chain reaction and recovery dates become the major visual moments.

Develop the detailed content outline only and stop for review before generating slides. This is for a class of ten-year-olds. Prioritize strong, specific, engaging content with a clear narrative, concrete explanations and examples, substantive age-appropriate copy, factual accuracy, and memorable teaching moments. Do not reuse any previously generated outline. Do not build or generate the deck until the user explicitly approves the plan.
